title: Mission 02: The Inventory
story: Word of your report recovery reached the director. Your reward: the department's neglected archive. Nobody knows what is in it, what is hiding in it, or what is newest, oldest or largest. Produce a complete inventory. ls will show you everything, if you know how to ask.

badge.name: The Inventory: Cataloged
badge.desc: Mastered ls by fully cataloging a messy department archive.

tasks.brief: Read BRIEFING2.txt in your department directory. Then, FROM your department directory, list the archive directory's visible contents into reports/inventory.txt (plain listing of archive, one name per line as ls produces when redirected).

checks.fail: reports/inventory.txt does not exist yet.
inventory.txt is not the plain listing of archive (run ls against archive from your department directory and redirect it).

tasks.brief: Some files in the archive start with a dot. Produce reports/all.txt: the SAME listing but with every hidden entry included.

checks.fail: reports/all.txt does not exist yet.
all.txt does not match the all-entries listing of archive (there is an ls option that stops hiding dotfiles).

tasks.brief: How many hidden entries live directly in archive (not counting the . and .. entries)? Write just that number on a single line to reports/hiddencount.txt.

checks.fail: reports/hiddencount.txt does not exist yet.
hiddencount.txt does not contain the right number of hidden entries (count dotfiles and dot-directories directly inside archive, excluding . and .. themselves).

tasks.brief: The director suspects one file is bloating the archive. Write the NAME of the largest file (by bytes, anywhere directly in archive's top level) to reports/largest.txt. ls can sort by size for you.

checks.fail: reports/largest.txt does not exist yet.
largest.txt does not name the biggest file in archive's top level (sort the listing by size and look at the top).

tasks.brief: Which top-level archive file was modified most recently? Its name goes in reports/newest.txt. ls can sort by time.

checks.fail: reports/newest.txt does not exist yet.
newest.txt does not name the most recently modified top-level file (sort the listing by modification time).

tasks.brief: And the fossil: the top-level archive file with the OLDEST modification time. Name it in reports/oldest.txt. The same time-sort can run in reverse.

checks.fail: reports/oldest.txt does not exist yet.
oldest.txt does not name the oldest top-level file (reverse the time-sorted listing, or read it from the bottom).

tasks.brief: Compliance wants the whole structure. FROM your department directory, produce reports/tree.txt: the RECURSIVE listing of archive (subdirectories and their contents included), exactly as ls renders it.

checks.fail: reports/tree.txt does not exist yet.
tree.txt does not match the recursive listing produced from your department directory against archive (use the relative name archive, not an absolute path, and let ls recurse).

tasks.brief: The auditor reads bottom-up. Produce reports/reverse.txt: archive's visible top-level listing in REVERSE name order.

checks.fail: reports/reverse.txt does not exist yet.
reverse.txt is not the reverse-name-order listing of archive (ls has a one-letter option for this).

tasks.brief: Just the folders: FROM your department directory, produce reports/dirs.txt listing ONLY the subdirectories of archive (the directory entries themselves, not their contents).

checks.fail: reports/dirs.txt does not exist yet.
dirs.txt should list only archive's subdirectory entries themselves (a shell glob ending in / plus the ls option that lists directories AS entries gets you there).
A professional keeps the reports directory free of scratch files.

tasks.brief: BONUS: two files in archive's top level are secretly the SAME file (two names, one inode). ls can show inode numbers. Write both names to reports/twins.txt, one per line, either order.

checks.fail: twins.txt must contain exactly the two hardlinked names, one per line (compare inode numbers in the listing).
